name: Maryland
uniformActsAdopted: Maryland Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (RUFADAA, 2016)
Maryland Revised Uniform Anatomical Gift Act (2011)
Uniform Adult Guardianship and Protective Proceedings Jurisdiction Act
note: Maryland is on the uniform acts for trusts, digital assets and anatomical gifts and on none of them for powers of attorney, probate or guardianship, and it is the state where the formality of an instrument depends entirely on which instrument it is. A financial power of attorney needs a notary, two witnesses and, if executed remotely, a supervising attorney who certifies what they saw; a health care agent can be appointed by a dated video file with no witnesses, or by speaking in front of a clinician. Two more Maryland particulars matter to this data: the small estate is a simplified administration with letters issued by the register of wills, not a collection by affidavit as in every other US jurisdiction here, and the certification that starts a health care agent's authority requires an examination within the previous two hours.

Acceptance of a statutory form power of attorney; liability for refusal
citations.quote: (a) A person may not require an additional or different form of power of attorney for any authority granted in a statutory form power of attorney. patches.diff:
Maryland's power of attorney act is its own, not the uniform one, despite what the enactment trackers suggest: title 17 is twenty sections against the Uniform Power of Attorney Act's fifty-odd, and it keeps the pre-uniform vocabulary of "attorney in fact". It nonetheless lands on the uniform **default**: § 17-105(c) makes a written power durable "unless otherwise provided by its terms", and § 17-105(b) applies that to all powers of attorney, overriding the carve-outs elsewhere in the title. So Maryland and Virginia, the two states either side of Delaware, both presume durability while Delaware presumes the opposite.

Execution is the strictest in this data. § 17-110 requires writing, signature, acknowledgement before a notary **and** attestation by **two or more adult witnesses**; Delaware wants a notary and one disinterested witness, Utah a notary. The remote route goes further than any other provision here: an electronic or remotely witnessed power of attorney needs the principal and every witness in the physical or electronic presence of one another **and of a supervising attorney**, the principal must be in or a resident of the State, each remote witness must be in the United States, and the supervising attorney must produce a **certified power of attorney** — a paper version of every page with a signed certification of what they observed. Maryland is the only jurisdiction in this set that makes a lawyer's participation a condition of a valid instrument.

The acceptance regime is narrower than Virginia's in a way worth recording. § 17-104 gives the same remedy — a court order mandating acceptance plus liability for reasonable attorney's fees and costs — but only for a **statutory form** power of attorney. A Maryland power drafted otherwise carries no duty to accept at all.

localNames: power of attorney limited by its terms
patches.diff: The exception in Maryland, and it has to be written into the instrument: a power is non-durable only where its terms provide for that (§ 17-105(c)). § 17-106 then protects the other side rather than the principal — the death, disability or incompetence of the principal does not revoke the agency as to an agent or other person who acts without actual knowledge of it, which is the pre-uniform form of the good-faith reliance rule.

Maryland departs from the baseline here by **omission**, which is the interesting part. Title 17 has no analogue of uniform § 109: nothing says when a power deferred to a future event becomes effective, and nothing names who determines that the event has occurred. Across all twenty sections of the title there is no determiner list of the kind Virginia (§ 64.2-1607), Delaware, Utah and Oklahoma all supply. What Maryland does define is **incapacity**, at § 17-101(g), and it defines it by reference to someone else's test: a principal is incapacitated if they meet the grounds for appointment of a guardian of the property under § 13-201, or are missing, detained, or outside the United States and unable to return. So the trigger is specified and the person who pulls it is not.

An agent appointed under the Maryland Health Care Decisions Act (Health-General title 5, subtitle 6), and Maryland's instrument is the most permissive in this entire data set — in three forms, two of which no other jurisdiction here recognises.

The ordinary form is written or electronic, dated, signed, and subscribed by **two witnesses** in the declarant's physical or electronic presence, at least one of whom is not knowingly entitled to any part of the estate or any benefit on the death (§ 5-602(c)(1), (2)).

The second is a **video record**. Under § 5-602(c)(3) the State-designated health information exchange may accept as valid an **unwitnessed** electronic advance directive in the form of a video record or file — to state the declarant's wishes **or to appoint an agent** — if it is dated and stored by an electronic advance directives service recognised by the Maryland Health Care Commission. An authority-conferring instrument here is a dated video file held by a designated intermediary, with no witness at all.

The third is **oral**. Under § 5-602(d) a competent individual may appoint an agent by an oral advance directive made in the presence of the attending physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner and one witness, provided its substance is documented in the medical record and the documentation is dated and signed by the clinician and the witness.

Authority commences on certification of incapacity (§ 5-602(e)), and Maryland's certification is the freshest-dated finding in this data: § 5-606 requires the attending physician **and** a second physician or nurse practitioner to certify in writing on personal examination, **one of whom must have examined the patient within 2 hours** before certifying. The second certification is excused where the patient is unconscious or cannot communicate.

Maryland's ladder under § 5-605(a)(2) is guardian, **spouse or domestic partner**, adult child, parent, adult sibling, then a friend or other relative — and a class may be reached only if everyone in the class above is "unavailable", a term the section defines to include a decision maker who cannot be found, who has not responded in a timely manner given the patient's needs, who is incapacitated, or who is unwilling to decide. Non-response moves the authority on.

The last class has to produce something, and Maryland's artefact is the third distinct answer in this data to the proof-of-standing question. A friend or other relative may act only on an **affidavit presented to the attending physician** stating that they are a relative or close friend and "specific facts and circumstances demonstrating that the person has maintained regular contact with the patient sufficient to be familiar with the patient's activities, health, and personal beliefs" — and § 5-605(5) requires the physician to **file that affidavit in the patient's medical record**. Utah prescribes a state form for its declaration; Delaware prescribes nothing; Virginia asks the claimant for nothing and makes a committee decide. Maryland asks for a sworn statement of specified content and then keeps it, so the evidence of standing becomes part of the record the relying party holds.

Disqualification is by relationship breakdown as well as abuse: a person subject to an interim, temporary or final protective order where the patient is eligible for relief may not decide, and nor may a spouse who has executed a separation agreement or where either has filed for divorce.

Appointment is by the court on petition under § 13-705, and Maryland sets the evidentiary bar expressly: **clear and convincing evidence** both that the person lacks sufficient understanding or capacity to make or communicate responsible personal decisions and that **no less restrictive form of intervention** is available consistent with their welfare and safety. Procedure and venue run through Title 10 of the Maryland Rules rather than the statute. Maryland has no version of the Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship and Other Protective Arrangements Act; title 13.5 is its adult-guardianship jurisdiction act, which decides which state may act rather than on what finding.

The property fiduciary in Maryland is a **guardian of the property**, not a conservator (§ 13-201), appointed for a minor who owns property needing management or for a person unable to manage their property effectively because of disability, disease, habitual drunkenness, addiction, imprisonment, compulsory hospitalisation, detention by a foreign power, or disappearance. That list is also what the power of attorney title borrows to define incapacity (§ 17-101(g)), so the same test starts a guardianship and triggers a springing power.

Maryland uses one name for both offices — **personal representative** — and one instrument, letters of administration, whether or not there is a will. The grant comes from the **register of wills**, an elected county officer, and the ordinary route is **administrative probate** under § 5-301: a proceeding instituted before the register, which "may be conducted **without prior notice**" and is final subject to an interested person's right to seek judicial probate. Judicial probate before the Orphans' Court follows only on request or where the petition is materially incomplete (§ 5-402).

That makes Maryland the strongest case in this set against assuming a court stands behind the grant: not merely a non-judicial officer issuing letters, as in Virginia, Delaware and Pennsylvania, but a whole probate proceeding conducted by that officer without notice to anyone. § 5-104 sets the priority, and its third class is the one to note: "the surviving spouse, **registered domestic partner**, and children of an intestate decedent".

Not a separate office in Maryland. The register grants letters of administration to a personal representative on a determination of intestacy in the same administrative probate proceeding that admits a will (§ 5-301), and § 5-104's priority list runs through both cases in one sequence. A credential asserting "holder is the personal representative" maps onto Maryland cleanly for that reason, where Delaware, Oklahoma and Virginia all name the artefact for the capacity in which it is held.

localNames: petitioner for administration of a small estate
patches.diff:
**Maryland has no affidavit route, and that is the finding.** Everywhere else in the US layer a small estate is collected without a grant, on a sworn statement presented to whoever holds the asset. In Maryland a small estate is a cheaper, faster **administration**: § 5-602 requires a petition for administration of a small estate, filed by a person entitled to letters under § 5-104, listing the known property, the known creditors with the amount of each claim, and any pending proceedings; and § 5-603 then has the **register direct the petitioner to serve as personal representative and issue letters of administration**, order payment of funeral expenses and the family allowance, and publish notice where property will remain. Bond is required above a $10,000 gross value and the personal representative takes no commissions.

The ceiling is **$50,000**, and it is the only one in this set that depends on who inherits rather than on the amount alone: § 5-601(c) raises it to **$100,000** where the surviving spouse is the sole legatee or heir. Idaho removes the ceiling entirely in that case; Maryland doubles it.

Maryland enacted the Uniform Trust Code as the **Maryland Trust Act** in 2014, at title 14.5 (§ 14.5-101). § 14.5-910 carries the uniform certification of trust, so a successor trustee's authority is evidenced by a certification the trustee signs rather than by anything a court issues.

The uniform mechanism, enacted in 2016. § 15-603(a) lets a user direct a custodian through an online tool to disclose to a designated recipient or not to disclose, and that direction overrides a contrary direction in a will, trust, power of attorney or other record provided the tool allows the user to modify or delete it **at any time**. Maryland's drafting of that proviso differs from the uniform "at all times" by a word and not in substance.

The Maryland Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act, self-titled at § 15-620 and running §§ 15-601 to 15-620 — the uniform act with the catalogue-and-content split, the four fiduciary types and the custodian provisions. One Maryland addition is worth recording because it is the only carve-out of its kind here: § 15-602 takes the whole subtitle out of play for "a digital asset of an employer used by an employee in the ordinary course of the employer's business", so a work account is outside the fiduciary-access regime altogether rather than being contested under it.

Maryland is on the Revised Uniform Anatomical Gift Act, self-titled at § 4-522 and sitting in the Estates and Trusts article rather than the health code. § 4-501 defines the agent as an individual authorised to make health care decisions by a power of attorney for health care or expressly authorised to make an anatomical gift, and § 4-504 governs amendment and revocation by a signed record or a later document of gift, including by another individual acting at the direction of a donor physically unable to sign.
